title: Codes, Patterns and Shapes of Contemporary Online Antisemitism and Conspiracy Narratives - an Annotation Guide and Labeled German-Language Dataset in the Context of COVID-19
measurement_description: The paper developed an annotation guide and a labeled dataset to detect and classify contemporary online antisemitism, including encoded forms, post-Holocaust antisemitism, and antisemitic conspiracy narratives within German-language Telegram messages related to the COVID-19 pandemic. It measured the prevalence and characteristics of antisemitic content and its overlap with conspiracy theories.
findings: The study found a significant overlap between antisemitism and conspiracy theories in their dataset, with over 72% of antisemitic texts also containing conspiracy content. A majority of the antisemitic content (almost 60%) was 'encoded,' using codes and metaphors rather than explicit terms. The most significant words correlated with antisemitic texts were references to Jewish identity (e.g., 'jew', 'jewish') and common antisemitic codes (e.g., 'illuminati', 'Soros', 'Rothschild', 'freemason', 'satanic'). The analysis highlights the importance of moving beyond simple keyword-based detection to identify these more subtle forms of hate speech.
